how_it_wins:
Let me tell you what the table thinks you're playing, and then what you're actually playing. They see an eight-mana commander and they relax. Good. Let them.

This deck is a two-act play, and Gishath, Sun's Avatar is only the second act. Act one is six quiet turns of ramp with a smile on your face: 35 lands, five rocks, three dorks, five land-ramp spells, three cost reducers. Meanwhile the deck assembles two engines, each one turning a single small event into a pile of material. You are not behind during those turns -- you are loading.

Engine one is the headline. When Gishath connects, you reveal that many cards, and every Dinosaur among them hits the battlefield free. That's not hope -- that's stack 001, which resolves one 7-damage connection into five new bodies, three Garruk's Uprising draws, and a Pantlaza discover at X=6. The sequencing lesson rides along: take the discover off your biggest toughness BEFORE any token enters, because Pantlaza's once-a-turn clause means the trigger you waste is a trigger you never get back.

Engine two doesn't need combat at all: the enrage ping web. With Forerunner of the Empire on the table, any Dinosaur entering lets you ping every creature for 1. Stack 005 shows one voluntary ping buying an exiled blocker (Trapjaw Tyrant), a card (Ripjaw Raptor), a land (Ranging Raptors), a fresh 5/5 (Polyraptor), and a dead opposing token -- all for damage that wipes off at cleanup. One ping, five payoffs, and the Polyraptor copy re-arms the trigger.

Now the coach's honesty, because I only promise wins I can deliver. The naked numbers say Gishath's mean cast turn is 7.969, and he's down by turn six in just 8.3% of simulated games. But that simulation can't even see Selvala, Regal Behemoth, or your reducers -- treat it as the floor of the problem, not your ceiling. What it CAN see is your act-one machinery firing: ramp in hand by turn six in 86.9% of games, the enrage engine in 72.6%, a Dinosaur payoff in 62.3%, a reducer or cheat piece in 56.2%.

Your job in act one is to spend that abundance while respecting the one thing that beats you: the board wipe. This deck deploys in one wave -- the trigger IS the wave -- so you swing big only with a shield held. You'll have one by turn six about 48.5% of the time; play like it's coming. When somebody does wipe you, rebuild the web first: it restarts at two cheap cards, while the commander plan restarts at eight plus tax.

And you have your own wipe that isn't really a wipe. Stack 004 verifies Blasphemous Act under Temple Altisaur and Wrathful Raptors as a one-sided apocalypse that throws 16 damage at a player on the way through.

Last thing, and this is your pregame speech. The bracket report computes a floor of 4, driven entirely by a database tag calling Polyraptor plus Forerunner a two-card infinite. Stack 003 put that tag under oath and it came back bounded: a maximum of SEVEN tokens, reached only by declining one trigger, and the chain kills its own engine on the third sweep. So you present the deck at 4 and you argue it at 3 -- out loud, before the game, with the verified line in hand.

That conversation isn't a weakness. That conversation is you running the table before a single land hits it.

combo_lines.001:
The court calls its favorite witness: Gishath's own text -- 'reveal that many cards from the top of your library. Put any number of Dinosaur creature cards from among them onto the battlefield.' Seven damage, seven cards, four Dinosaurs, and nine triggered abilities all demanding a place on the stack.

The clause that decides the whole case is Pantlaza's rider, 'Do this only once each turn.' Per CR 603.2h, that rider polices the TRIGGERING itself, not merely the payoff. Once you've discovered this turn, later entries don't produce a trigger at all -- the ability simply declines to appear.

So the holding, plain enough to carry to any table: you control the order. Put the Carnage Tyrant discover on top and the Regisaur Alpha token on the bottom -- discover at X=6 first, token last, and the token enters into a world where Pantlaza has nothing left to say. Misorder it and you discover at X=3 instead. Perfectly legal, and strictly worse -- the rules punish nothing here except carelessness.
combo_lines.002:
A cautionary case, and a standing verdict this court is proud of. The exhibit is CR 732.4 with 104.4b: a loop of mandatory actions that no player can stop does not win the game -- it DRAWS the game, for everyone.

Read the two texts side by side and savor the absence. Marauding Raptor's ping is 'deals 2 damage to it' -- no 'may.' Polyraptor's enrage is 'create a token' -- no 'may.' Two damage never kills a fresh 5/5 token, each new token enters clean and gets pinged exactly once, and this deck fields no sacrifice outlet and no free exit.

Resolve Polyraptor with Marauding Raptor on the battlefield and you have not assembled a win. You have filed a motion to dismiss the entire game -- granted automatically unless an opponent chooses to intervene, on their terms, at a token count they select, most cleanly by killing the Raptor.

The holding: the combo database calls this pair an infinite; the record calls it a liability. That is the whole reason Marauding Raptor resides in the sideboard while Polyraptor plays -- and any future reunion requires a loop-breaker to be sleeved first.
combo_lines.003:
The case that decides your bracket conversation. Exhibit one, CR 603.5: an optional triggered ability's choice is made on resolution. Every one of Forerunner of the Empire's sweeps asks 'you may,' and you answer each time, in the moment. Which means this so-called infinite has a steering wheel and a brake.

The finding, verified step by step: the ceiling is SEVEN Polyraptor tokens -- eight Polyraptors counting the original. Reaching seven requires the connoisseur's move of DECLINING one intermediate trigger so a token enters before the final sweep; say yes to everything like an amateur and you cap at six. The chain then closes its own file: Forerunner's third sweep is its own third point of damage, and the 1/3 is destroyed by the very engine it was running.

The holding: bounded above by seven, terminated by its own operation, stoppable at every single link. When the combo database testifies 'infinite,' this record is your cross-examination. Present the deck at bracket 4, argue it at 3, and enter stack 003 into evidence.
combo_lines.004:
My favorite kind of case: one where the deceased gives testimony. Blasphemous Act deals 13 to each of nine creatures as a single event. Temple Altisaur's prevention shield -- 'all but 1' -- covers every Dinosaur you control EXCEPT the one drafting the policy: Altisaur is not 'another Dinosaur' to itself, takes the full 13, and dies.

But observe CR 113.7a, the finest clause in the book: a trigger whose source has left the battlefield resolves using last known information. The dead Altisaur was a Dinosaur dealt 13, so Wrathful Raptors throws 13 on its behalf. Better still, CR 704.5g clears every lethally-wounded creature off the battlefield BEFORE the redirect triggers choose targets -- the opponents' creatures are already gone, so the only legal non-Dinosaur targets left are players.

Sixteen damage upstairs, a Ripjaw card drawn, your board intact minus one noble martyr. The holding: the killing blow still triggers, and the dead still owe testimony. Your board wipe is the only one at the table that comes with a forwarding address.
combo_lines.005:
The everyday case -- the one you'll litigate most turns from midgame on. Exhibit: CR 704.3, which orders state-based actions performed before any waiting trigger is placed on the stack; and CR 603.5 again, every link a 'you may.'

One Dinosaur enters, you accept one Forerunner ping, and the docket fills. The opposing 1/1 is dead by state-based action before you even choose targets. Trapjaw Tyrant exiles their 3/3 -- a hostage, held until Trapjaw leaves.

Ripjaw Raptor draws; that one's mandatory, the court's gift. Ranging Raptors fetches a tapped Forest. Polyraptor files a fresh 5/5 copy, and the copy's own entry re-arms Forerunner with a genuinely new, genuinely optional trigger. Decline it and you bank the full yield with no further self-harm.

Note for the record: Itzquinth carries no enrage -- it is the witness that summoned the court, not a beneficiary. The holding: one voluntary point of damage, marked until cleanup and then forgiven, buys removal, ramp, a card, and a body. Say yes for exactly as long as the price is right.

card_roles.Gishath, Sun's Avatar: The whole franchise: vigilance, trample, haste, and a connect that turns 7 damage into a free board. Stack 001 clocks one hit at five bodies, three draws, and a discover 6. The play: swing only with a shield held or a lane cleared. The trap: every death adds two to an eight-mana bill.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: With your commander out you take BOTH modes -- protection and lethal evasion in one card. Hold it for the swing turn; it's also one of the only shields that covers Forerunner of the Empire, your non-Dinosaur engine hub.
card_roles.Alpine Meadow: Tapped R/W snow dual. Play it on a turn the mana wasn't working anyway -- never on the turn before the big cast.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any commander color, no questions asked. Deploy by turn three; your land drops fade late (52.6% by turn six), and rocks are the difference.
card_roles.Austere Command: The sweeper that lets you choose survivors -- 'artifacts plus mana value 3 or less' usually clears their board and your guilt. The trap: pick greedy modes and your own rocks and dorks go with them.
card_roles.Beast Within: Answers ANY permanent at instant speed. The 3/3 you hand back is pocket change at a table where your average body is twice its size.
card_roles.Belbe's Portal: Name Dinosaur; then 3 and a tap flashes any one from hand -- ambush blockers, dodge sorcery removal. The trap is the mana: Unclaimed Territory casts spells only and Secluded Courtyard pays creature sources only, so neither typal land ever funds this activation.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Your catch-up button, and with Temple Altisaur plus Wrathful Raptors out it's a verified one-sided apocalypse that throws 16 at a player on the way through (stack 004). The trap: Altisaur eats its own 13 and dies -- budget for the martyr.
card_roles.Bonehoard Dracosaur: Every upkeep: two free cards to play plus a token either way. First strike and flying hold the fort while it pays for your turns. Trap: it exiles your top two -- mind any top-of-library setup you've stacked.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Two mana, three jobs: indestructible through a wrath, four at a face, or double strike on the big one. The cheapest wrath insurance in the 99 -- hold it like it's worth the whole board, because it is.
card_roles.Boros Signet: R/W on demand. Filters colorless rock mana into your two toughest pips.
card_roles.Bronzebeak Foragers: Enters and takes a hostage from EACH opponent -- three-for-one removal on a Dinosaur body Gishath can put in free. The trap: they're hostages, not corpses. If the Foragers leave, everything comes home unless you've paid the X ability first.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: G/W, untapped once you control two basics. With fourteen basics in the list, that's most of the game.
card_roles.Carnage Tyrant: Can't be countered, can't be targeted, tramples for seven -- the payoff the control seat cannot answer on the stack. Stack 001's line discovers off its toughness for X=6; it's the best name you can see in a reveal.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: R/G, untapped with two basics under you. Sequence your basics early and it's a real dual.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any color, one life. Pay it happily -- a missed pip costs more than a point ever will.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: R/W, untapped if you hold a Mountain or Plains. A check land in a deck with typed duals passes the check often.
card_roles.Command Tower: The best land in the format doing the best-land things. No play pattern, no trap, just gratitude.
card_roles.Congregation at Dawn: Stack your top three creatures at instant speed, then let Gishath connect: three hand-picked Dinosaurs, free. The trap: any shuffle or top-of-library exile (Bonehoard's upkeep included) torches the setup. Cast it when the connect is imminent, not aspirational.
card_roles.Cultivate: One land down, one land in hand -- ramp plus the future land drop this deck starts missing by midgame. A turn-three staple you're never sad to see.
card_roles.Curious Altisaur: Every Dinosaur that connects draws you a card -- combat converted to fuel -- and reach means it holds off fliers while doing it. Attack wide, read the cards.
card_roles.Descendants' Path: Free upkeep casts off your top for any creature sharing a type with your board -- in a list this thick with Dinosaurs, it hits plenty. The trap: a miss bottoms the revealed card, so it can eat a top you carefully stacked.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your whole team past a wrath and re-buy every enters trigger on the way home. The trap: tokens exiled this way are gone for good -- Polyraptor copies don't ride the interlude.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana, any artifact or enchantment to your top: Urza's Incubator when you need the discount, Mirari's Wake when you need the world, Garruk's Uprising when you need the engine. Cast it end-step and draw into the answer.
card_roles.Etali, Primal Storm: Each attack exiles the top of EVERY library and casts the hits free -- a value engine that scales with the table's card quality, not yours. Give it haste (Otepec, Regisaur) and it pays off the turn it lands.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Any color an opponent's land could make -- at a three-color table it's a Command Tower with a scouting report. The trap is real but rare: against all-colorless boards it's a blank.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: FREE with your commander out: indestructible for the team while you're tapped out on the Gishath turn -- exactly the shield the plan orders. Also covers Forerunner; that duty matters.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any color, every time, and the opponent gets a 1/1 Spirit. The trap: you're arming chump blockers -- point them at the seat you aren't attacking.
card_roles.Forest: The basic your eleven Forest-fetchers are all looking for. Seven copies; sequence them to turn on the check duals and battle lands.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Board-wide trample plus a card for every 4-power body -- stack 001 shows exactly three draws off one connect. Know the cutoff: 3-power tokens (Regisaur's, Huatli's) don't draw. Power four is the bar; most of your roster clears it.
card_roles.Ghalta and Mavren: Every attack: either a giant tapped-and-attacking Dinosaur or a lifelink token army, your pick, free, forever. It's value stapled to the thing you were doing anyway. The trap: the token Dinosaur enters attacking -- it never blocks for you.
card_roles.Ghalta, Primal Hunger: Reads twelve mana, costs about three with a real board -- a 12/12 trample finisher priced like a midrange play. The discount is cast-only; in a Gishath reveal it's simply free, which is even better.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana: hexproof AND indestructible for everything you control. It answers the wrath, the targeted exile, the theft spell -- the one-card reason to always leave G-1 up on your big turns.
card_roles.Huatli, Poet of Unity // Roar of the Fif: Front side fixes: a basic to hand on entry. Five mana later she flips into a Saga that makes two 3/3s, teaches your whole team to tap for mana, tutors a Dinosaur, and closes on team double strike and trample. Flip her the turn before you intend to end someone.
card_roles.Hulking Raptor: Ward 2 on a real body that adds GG every one of your first mains -- a ramp 'dork' the removal spell has to pay extra to answer. It accelerates Gishath by a full turn all by itself.
card_roles.Hunter's Insight: Aim it at an unblocked Gishath and draw SEVEN on top of the reveal. The play: cast it after blockers are declared, never before -- you're paying for certainty, so buy certainty.
card_roles.Intrepid Paleontologist: Any-color dork, graveyard hate, and a recursion outlet that casts Dinosaurs out of exile -- three jobs on a two-drop. The trap: finality counters mean each recovered Dinosaur gets exactly one more life; spend it well.
card_roles.Itzquinth, Firstborn of Gishath: Hasty two-drop that can pay 2 on entry to have your best Dinosaur snipe a creature -- removal shaped like a body. Note from stack 005: it carries no enrage of its own; it's the trigger that starts the web, not a payoff inside it.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: All three colors, tapped -- and when the game goes long, cycling turns the spare land into a card. Early land drop or late cantrip; never a dead draw.
card_roles.Kessig Wolf Run: A colorless land until it's the kill: X plus RG gives one creature +X and trample. Every spare Polyraptor token is one activation away from being a problem nobody blocked for.
card_roles.Kodama's Reach: Cultivate's twin -- land down, land in hand. Redundancy in the effect your whole schedule leans on is a feature, not a filler.
card_roles.Krosan Verge: Sacrifices into a Forest AND a Plains -- and typed duals like Canopy Vista and Jetmir's Garden count. Two lands from one drop, exactly what a 52.6% turn-six land-drop rate wants. It enters tapped; play it early, crack it at leisure.
card_roles.Mirari's Wake: Team +1/+1 and every land taps for double -- the turn after it sticks, your eight-drops cost like five-drops. It's the enchantment Enlightened Tutor fetches when the plan is 'go over everyone.'
card_roles.Monster Manual // Zoological Study: 1G and a tap puts a creature from hand into play -- the budget Portal, with an adventure side that mills five and retrieves a creature first. Same mana trap as the Portal: the typal lands can't pay the activation. Real mana only.
card_roles.Mountain: Four copies of the humble red pip. Turns on Cinder Glade, Clifftop Retreat, and Rootbound Crag just by existing.
card_roles.Myriad Landscape: Sacrifices into two basics of a shared type -- a land that becomes two. Tapped at every stage, so start the clock early.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: A Forest onto the battlefield UNTAPPED, and typed duals qualify -- turn two Nature's Lore into Canopy Vista is fixing and ramp in one. The Forest-typed count in this list is eleven; the hit rate is the point.
card_roles.Otepec Huntmaster: Dinosaurs cost 1 less and something gets haste every turn, free. It's the card that makes a discovered Carnage Tyrant swing NOW. The trap: it's a 1/1 Human -- it dies to a stiff breeze and your own Blasphemous Act alike.
card_roles.Overwhelming Stampede: +X/+X and trample where X is your biggest power -- with a Gishath or Ghalta on board that's the table-ending math. The closer you cast AFTER the reveal fills the board, not before.
card_roles.Pantlaza, Sun-Favored: Every Dinosaur entering may discover X equal to its toughness, once per turn -- the engine that keeps producing the turn after a wrath, no combat and no eight mana required. The trap is sequencing, verified in stack 001: take the discover off your biggest toughness BEFORE any token enters. Once it's used, later entries don't even trigger.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Any commander color, tapped, and a scry on nearly every creature you cast -- Gishath is a Dinosaur Avatar, so most of the roster qualifies. Small edges, every turn, forever.
card_roles.Path to Exile: One mana, exile anything. The basic land you hand over is a real cost early -- so spend this on the creature that actually threatens the plan, not the first thing that annoys you.
card_roles.Plains: Three copies of the white anchor. Windswept Heath, Krosan Verge, and the check lands all come looking for it.
card_roles.Pugnacious Hammerskull: A 6/5 for three mana that just attacks people. The one honest trap on the card: alone it stuns itself -- swing it only with a second Dinosaur on the field, which in this deck is a low bar.
card_roles.Quartzwood Crasher: Trample connects mint X/X trample Dinosaurs equal to the damage dealt -- and Garruk's Uprising gives EVERYTHING trample, so every combat compounds. Left alone for two turns it builds its own army.
card_roles.Regal Imperiosaur: A three-mana lord: every other Dinosaur gets +1/+1. Quietly moves half your roster past sweep math and combat math at once.
card_roles.Regisaur Alpha: The team gets haste, and it brings a 3/3 trample friend on arrival -- the best name to see in a reveal when you want the new board swinging next turn. Stack 001's fine print: haste doesn't grant a second combat; it's insurance for the NEXT swing, not this one.
card_roles.Ripjaw Raptor: Enrage: dealt damage, draw a card -- verified drawing live in stacks 004 and 005. A 4/5 that profits from blocking, from your own pings, from the table's spite. Let it get hit; that's the business model.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: Draw cards equal to your biggest power, then cast something five-or-less for free -- with any giant out, that's a refilled hand plus a free Regisaur Alpha. Cast it the turn after a reveal, when your power is embarrassing.
card_roles.Rogue's Passage: Four mana and a tap: Gishath cannot be blocked. The connection is the entire deck; this land is the guarantee. The kit it belongs to is in hand by turn six about half the time (51.4%); save the activation for the turn that matters.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: R/G, untapped with a Mountain or Forest under you -- and this deck nearly always qualifies.
card_roles.Secluded Courtyard: Name Dinosaur: any color for Dinosaur spells AND for abilities of Dinosaur creatures -- read the clause, it's more generous than its reputation. Still can't fund Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual; artifacts aren't creature sources.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: TWO Forests onto the battlefield untapped -- and typed duals count, so it can fetch Canopy Vista plus Cinder Glade and fix everything at once. The best pure ramp spell in the 99; the four-mana price is the whole trap.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Sol Ring. Turn one if the game loves you; there is no bad turn for it.
card_roles.Sunpetal Grove: G/W, untapped with a Forest or Plains -- the check this deck passes in its sleep.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana, exile the problem, and the life they gain never blocked anybody. Premier removal; spend it on commanders and engines, not on bodies you can out-body.
card_roles.Talisman of Unity: G/W rock with an optional point of pain -- take the damage when the color matters, take the colorless when it doesn't. On the table by turn two is the assignment.
card_roles.Temple Altisaur: The enrage governor: every damage source hits your OTHER Dinosaurs for exactly 1. Sweepers become upside, big blocks become jokes, and every ping still turns enrage on. Two traps, both verified in stack 004: it never protects itself, and it never covers Forerunner -- a Human is not a Dinosaur.
card_roles.Thrashing Brontodon: A 3/4 that sacrifices at instant speed to kill any artifact or enchantment -- interaction that attacks in the meantime. Hold the activation for the piece that actually locks you out.
card_roles.Topiary Stomper: Ramp on a 4/4 body: a basic straight to the battlefield on entry. The trap is printed right on it -- it can't attack or block until you control seven lands, so early on it's a vegetable with a pension plan. That's fine; you hired it for the land.
card_roles.Triumphant Chomp: One red mana: damage equal to your biggest Dinosaur's power -- in this deck, that's a one-mana kill spell most turns. The trap: it's a sorcery, so the ambush window everyone imagines isn't there.
card_roles.Trumpeting Carnosaur: Discover 5 on entry, or discard it any time for 3 damage to a creature or planeswalker -- a six-drop that is never a dead card in any hand at any stage. The flexibility IS the role.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Any color -- for Dinosaur SPELLS, full stop. The deck-facts warning stands: this mana never activates Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, or anything else. It accelerates the cast plan and only the cast plan.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: Dinosaurs cost 2 less -- across 34 bodies that's the biggest mana discount in the deck, and it drags Gishath's arrival forward all by itself. Enlightened Tutor's first-choice fetch when the hand is full of fat.
card_roles.Vaultborn Tyrant: Three life and a card every time a 4-power body enters -- including itself -- and when it dies it leaves a copy behind. The grind engine that makes attrition tables regret their life choices.
card_roles.Wakening Sun's Avatar: Destroy all non-Dinosaur creatures -- a board wipe you're on the right side of. The trap is the headline: it only fires when CAST FROM HAND, so a Gishath reveal or a Portal drop skips the wipe entirely. This one you pay for the honest way, on purpose.
card_roles.Wayward Swordtooth: An extra land drop every turn for two mana -- fuel for a deck whose drops thin out by midgame. Yes, it needs the city's blessing to fight; no, you don't care. You hired it for the land drops, and ten permanents arrives sooner than you think.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One green mana: any creature to your top. Cast it with a Gishath connect incoming and it reads 'put the best Dinosaur in the deck onto the battlefield.' The cleanest setup spell in the list.
card_roles.Zacama, Primal Calamity: Nine mana that untaps your lands when CAST, so it's nearly free the turn it resolves. Then it's a removal machine: 3 damage, artifact/enchantment kill, or lifegain on demand. The trap: cheated into play (a reveal, a Portal), no untap -- 'if you cast it' means exactly that.
card_roles.Selvala, Heart of the Wilds: Taps for X equal to your greatest power -- with any 5-power Dinosaur out, that's Gishath years ahead of schedule. She also draws you cards when your biggest bodies land. The trap: every experienced table kills her on sight; deploy her when you can use the mana immediately, not a turn early.
card_roles.Regal Behemoth: Monarch on entry, and while you hold the crown every land taps for an extra mana of any color -- a mana engine wearing a 5/5 trample body. The trap: the crown paints the target; expect the table to come collect, and welcome the extra card each turn they don't.
card_roles.Forerunner of the Empire: The web's hub: entry puts any Dinosaur on top of your library to feed the next reveal, and every Dinosaur ETB may ping ALL creatures for 1 -- the switch that turns enrage on (stacks 003 and 005). The traps, all verified: it's a 1/3 HUMAN -- outside Temple Altisaur's shield, outside the typal lands' mana, never free-rolled by Gishath's reveal -- and its own sweep hits it. Protect the Human; the board-wide instants are its only cover.
card_roles.Polyraptor: Enrage: dealt damage, build another Polyraptor. One ping, one fresh 5/5 (stack 005); the full Forerunner burst caps at seven tokens and shuts itself off (stack 003). The one trap that matters: never share a battlefield with Marauding Raptor without an exit -- that loop is mandatory and it draws the whole game (stack 002).
card_roles.Wrathful Raptors: Every point your Dinosaurs take gets thrown at something that isn't one. Stack 004 verifies the ceiling: under Blasphemous Act with Temple Altisaur out, it converts a board wipe into 16 damage upstairs. One honest unknown: its interaction with the Forerunner ping web on the same board is unverified rules territory -- don't promise yourself the enrage yield with both out until it's resolved.
card_roles.Ranging Raptors: Enrage ramp: every ping fetches a tapped basic (verified live in stack 005). A 2/3 that turns damage -- yours, theirs, anybody's -- into land drops the deck badly wants.
card_roles.Trapjaw Tyrant: Enrage removal: every ping exiles an opponent's creature -- verified, repeatable, one ping one hostage (stack 005). The trap: exiles last only while Trapjaw lives; when it leaves, everything comes home at once. Track your hostages.
card_roles.Windswept Heath: One life: any Forest or Plains card, typed duals included -- fixing, thinning, and battle-land enablement in one crack. Crack it at end of turn unless you need the mana now.
card_roles.Commercial District: Tapped R/G with a surveil on entry -- a free look that can bin a dead top card before an upkeep reveal. Small filter, right colors.
card_roles.Arctic Treeline: Tapped G/W snow dual. Same rule as every tapped land here: it goes down on the cheap turns, never before the big one.

mulligan:
Hand clinic. Fall in, and smile -- the numbers are on your side. The simulation keeps 77.1% of opening sevens and averages 0.28 mulligans a game, so this deck WANTS to keep. Your whole job is spotting the minority of hands that are lying to you.

KEEP: two to four lands plus at least one act-one card -- a ramp spell, a rock, a dork, or a web piece. That's the drill. Here's why it works: ramp shows up by turn six in 86.9% of games and the enrage engine in 72.6%, so a hand that starts the machine gets reinforcements. A hand with Cultivate, a Signet, and a Ranging Raptors is a GOOD hand even with nothing flashy in it -- you're not keeping cards, you're keeping a schedule.

SHIP: any hand whose plan is 'draw Gishath and pray.' He arrives on a mean turn of 7.969 and he's out by turn six in 8.3% of games -- the big man is act two, and a hand full of eight-drops is a hand full of act two. Ship zero- and one-landers without ceremony; the model itself refuses anything outside two-to-five lands, and so do you. Ship five-plus lands with no engine piece -- that hand ramps into nothing.

The judgment calls, with teeth. A four-land keep is fine, not flood: your land drops dry up fast (only 52.6% of games are still hitting the drop on turn six, mean mana 5.486 by then), so extra lands early are the budget you'll be glad you banked. Don't mulligan hunting for protection -- you'll hold a shield by turn six in about half your games (48.5%). Keep the hand that builds a board worth shielding, and hold the shield when it shows.

And never, ever ship a hand because it 'only' has small Dinosaurs in it. Ranging Raptors and Ripjaw Raptor are not small. They're the engine wearing a modest jersey.
upgrades:
Here's how the ten below got picked, because a ranked list is only as honest as its assembly line. The bench went under the lamp first: twenty-one fair, conditional bodies, and exactly four earn a slot by plugging into engines the stacks verify — the lead extends the stack 005 ping web directly. The other six are scouted from the pool to fill gaps the indexes flag. Each one beat the bench tail on a claim the tail couldn't match: a verified-stack extension, an index entry, or a role the budget says the deck is short.

Read the evidence tags like a balance sheet. A stack number next to a claim is settled money — the line already resolved under the checker. A goldfish or index figure is reproducible arithmetic: solid, but it measures the deck as built, not the deck plus the new card. And 'needs a stack scenario' is a promissory note — the biggest ceilings on this list carry that flag, and you don't book a ceiling until the scenario runs.

Every entry names its natural cut and its bracket delta, and one number frames all ten: none of them moves the computed floor off 4. The floor rides the combo database's Polyraptor-plus-Forerunner tag, and stack 003 bounds that pair at seven tokens — so you're shopping for power inside a bracket you've already argued. Buy in rank order if you want my order; buy for your pod if you know your pod.
mana_base:
Twenty-four lands, and twelve of them enter tapped. That's a 50% tap rate against the one-in-three budget the deck builder allows itself — every other land drop hands back a tempo beat, and the deck signs for it because three-colour fixing under a curve this top-heavy doesn't come free. Know the bill: tapped lands go down on the cheap turns, never the one before the big cast.

Now the disagreement the audit exists to surface. Green writes 56.2% of the pips in this deck but holds only 35.9% of the sources. The lands split almost evenly — 14 green, 13 red, 12 white — while the demand doesn't split at all. Red runs the opposite book, 19.8% of pips on 33.3% of sources; when a hand stalls on colour, it stalls on green.

The on-curve numbers price it. Lands alone, you make your pips on schedule 37.3% of the time in green, 33.6% in red, 29.9% in white. Fold in the rocks and dorks and those climb to 58%, 48.1%, and 51.5% — the nonland producers aren't garnish, they're carrying close to half the load. Protect the Signets and the dorks accordingly; the sweep that takes them takes a third of your mana base.

Here's what the five rocks, three dorks, and five land-ramp spells actually buy. The goldfish puts ramp in hand by turn six in 86.9% of games and mean available mana at 7.321 by turn ten — a figure 24 lands could never post alone. The ramp package is the difference between casting Gishath and reading about him.

One last number, so nobody misreads the tables: the 90% on-curve yardstick works out to 36 sources per colour, and this deck fields 14 green land sources at its richest. That target is unreachable by design in a 24-land ramp deck — the audit isn't grading you against it, it's pricing the gap. The gap is the plan; the ramp spells are the payments.
threat_assessment:
Here's what the table sees when you sit down: an eight-mana commander in the command zone and a player they figure they can ignore for seven turns. They're reading the clock right — Gishath's mean cast turn is 7.969, median 8, on the battlefield by turn 6 in just 8.3% of goldfish games. They're reading the seat completely wrong. That gap is where you win, and your first six turns exist to keep it open.

Start winning before the deck is cut. The pregame conversation is yours to run, so run it like a closer — smile on, receipts out. The bracket report computes a floor of 4. Say so first; never let someone else break your own news.

Then show your work. The entire jump from 3 to 4 rides one driver: the combo database tags Polyraptor plus Forerunner of the Empire as a two-card infinite. Your checker resolved that exact pairing on a real board (stack 003, verdict: pass). The verified ceiling is seven Polyraptor tokens — a number you only reach by DECLINING an intermediate trigger, because saying yes to everything caps at six.

The chain stops itself when Forerunner dies to its own third sweep, and every link is a 'you may.' Bounded, controllable, done. The famously unbounded partner, Marauding Raptor, is not in your 99. And stack 002 (verdict: pass) shows that pairing isn't even a win — it's a mandatory whole-table DRAW under CR 732.4 and 104.4b.

Present the 4, argue the 3, and let the table land where the evidence points. That conversation is not an apology. It's the bracket system working — and it's your first scouting report on who at this table does their homework.

Then become the most boring player in the room, on purpose. Ramp or fixing is in your hand by turn 6 in 86.9% of games (mean turn 2.0), so you always have a quiet, legitimate play — a Cultivate, a Signet, a lone 2/3.

Meanwhile the real engine assembles in plain sight. The enrage web is drawn by turn 6 in 72.6% of games, and its output doesn't read as aggression. One optional Forerunner ping (stack 005, verdict: pass) converts a single Dinosaur entering into a dead opposing token, their best creature exiled under Trapjaw Tyrant, a Ripjaw Raptor card, a Ranging Raptors Forest, and a fresh 5/5 Polyraptor that re-arms the trigger. Nobody at the table calls the archenemy over a tapped Forest.

Bank it all. Every ping is permanent value the eventual wrath cannot repossess.

Know your tells, because the table is watching for them. Three things flip you from wallpaper to archenemy. One: casting Gishath — they counted to eight with you. Two: connecting once — stack 001 turns seven damage into five bodies, three draws, and a discover at X=6, and nobody un-sees that.

Three: Polyraptor standing next to Forerunner. The database lists that pairing in 12,132 decks; anyone with a phone knows its reputation, deserved or not.

So never drift onto the throne — choose the moment. The pivot checklist is three boxes: Gishath castable, a protection instant in hand, and a seat that cannot profitably block or answer. You hold a protection instant by turn 6 in 48.5% of games — check before you commit.

Selvala, Heart of the Wilds and Regal Behemoth can drag that turn forward; Selvala taps for X equal to your greatest power, which any 5/5 makes 5. But remember the crown paints you. Take the monarchy when you're ready to be looked at.

And protect your franchise player. Forerunner of the Empire is a 1/3 Human Soldier running a Dinosaur company, and every tribal benefit in the building walks right past him.

Count the misses. Temple Altisaur prevents damage to OTHER Dinosaurs. Secluded Courtyard and Unclaimed Territory name Dinosaur. Gishath's reveal only free-rolls Dinosaurs, and Descendants' Path will never flip him up.

His own sweep hits him too — verified at 1 of his 3 toughness in stack 005, and dead to his own third sweep in stack 003. The only umbrellas that cover him are your board-wide instants: Flawless Maneuver, Heroic Intervention, Boros Charm, Akroma's Will, or an Eerie Interlude blink. So deploy him the turn he works, not a turn early. A sharp opponent kills the 1/3 before the 7/6.

When all three boxes check and the moment comes: cast, connect, bank the trigger, and welcome the coalition. You didn't spend six turns under the radar to flinch on turn eight. Archenemy with a stocked board and a free Maneuver is exactly the job this deck was built to hold.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL — the toughest seat at the table, so scout it hardest and walk in with the plan. Your board arrives as one wrath-sized package; deploying in waves is structurally off the menu, because the Gishath trigger IS the wave. So make every sweeper pay retail. Swing only with a board-wide instant held — Flawless Maneuver is free while your commander is on the battlefield — and aim the pivot at the turn the control player taps low.

You hold that protection by turn 6 in 48.5% of games. In the games you don't, you're not stalled — you're accruing. The ping web's yield banks permanently: Ranging Raptors' Forests stay on the battlefield, and Ripjaw Raptor's cards stay in your hand, through any wrath ever printed.

Know your exposure honestly. Land-drop hit rate falls to 52.6% by turn 6 and mean available mana is 5.486, so mid-game you're riding rocks and dorks a hard sweep can take with it. Favor the land ramp — Cultivate, Kodama's Reach, Nature's Lore — into a suspected wrath turn.

And when the board does get cleared, look at the price tags. Their next wrath costs a whole card; your rebuild costs two. Forerunner plus any Dinosaur restarts the entire web, and Pantlaza discovers again off the very next body while Gishath waits at 8 plus tax. One note for the ledger: Trapjaw Tyrant's hostage comes home when Trapjaw leaves, so count that creature in your post-wrath math.

You out-grind the control seat by making every wrath a losing trade. A control deck that can't trade profitably is a deck playing YOUR game.

VS FASTER COMBO — the honest scouting report: they're faster. Honest is where winning starts. Naya hands you zero counterspells; your interaction is 6 spot-removal slots and 2 sweepers, and your natural clock starts turns 6 through 8. So play the underdog with a puncher's chance — which you are, and which is enough.

Answer economy first. Spend removal on enablers the moment they hit the table. A Beast Within held for a hypothetical is a Beast Within that never stopped anything.

You are the beatdown in every one of these games, no matter how controlling your ramp turns feel. Act like it.

Selvala, Heart of the Wilds and Regal Behemoth are your nitro. The 7.969 mean cast turn is a simulation that models neither card (stated goldfish assumption) — treat it as the floor of your speed, not the ceiling. One Selvala activation at X=5 off any 5/5 collapses the math.

The web sharpens the race too. Every Dinosaur entering with Forerunner out is a token for the clock and a Trapjaw exile aimed at whatever blocks (stack 005). Force them to combo under pressure with removal up — combo decks are built to win comfortable, and your job is to make sure they never are.

VS STAX — taxes hit an 8-drop hardest, so don't play the 8-drop's game until you've broken theirs. Here's what I love about your seat: the ping web runs on creature ETBs. No activations, no big casts — nothing a Winter-Orb table meaningfully taxes (stated archetypal assumption: sphere effects and activation taxes, not creature bans). And Selvala compresses your whole mana development into one activation.

Mulligan toward the cheat layer: Urza's Incubator, Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual, Descendants' Path, and Huatli, Poet of Unity. One is in hand by turn 6 in 56.2% of games.

Now the trap, named before you step in it. Unclaimed Territory's mana casts creature spells ONLY — it can never activate Portal or Manual. Secluded Courtyard pays only creature-source abilities, which those artifacts are not. Both typal lands accelerate the cast plan, never the cheat plan; budget real mana for the activations.

Spend your six spot-removal slots on the one piece that turns off your cheat layer specifically, not the piece that annoys you most. You field 34 must-answer bodies; a stax engine is load-bearing on maybe three cards. Break one and walk through the door they were paid to hold shut.

VS ENRAGE-HOSTILE BOARDS — the go-wide tables you can't race, and the boards that punish a ping. Against the swarm, you're holding the verified trump card. Stack 004 (verdict: pass) resolves Blasphemous Act under Temple Altisaur and Wrathful Raptors: your Dinosaurs are each DEALT exactly 1 and live, state-based actions clear the opponents' creatures before redirect targets are chosen, and every redirect goes at a face. The verified run put 16 damage into one player — 40 down to 10 — plus a Ripjaw draw.

Budget the one casualty. Temple Altisaur is not 'another Dinosaur' to itself, eats its own 13, and still converts death into a 13-point redirect via last known information. And the wider they go, the cheaper it gets — Blasphemous Act costs {1} less per creature on the battlefield.

Against boards that turn pings hostile — assume an opponent whose creatures have their own dealt-damage payoffs — remember the web's greatest feature: every single link is a 'you may.' Forerunner's sweep hits ALL creatures, theirs included. When the exchange favors you — their x/1 tokens die, their best blocker gets Trapjawed — ping freely. When it feeds them, decline and lose nothing; that's verified in stack 005, where declining the re-armed trigger closed the turn with the full yield banked.

Your marked damage clears at every cleanup. Their board doesn't come back from an exile. And the board that hates your pings is exactly the board Blasphemous Act loves. Either way, you're holding the better end of the mathematics — play it like you know it.
